turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on in, I'll grab your vitals real quick before he sits down with you.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, yeah. Sorry we're a little late, the parking garage was full and then the elevator stopped on every floor, and I was already sneezing in there which was, um, embarrassing.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): You're fine. Blood pressure is one eighteen over seventy four. Heart rate seventy two. Oxygen sat ninety eight percent.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Last time the pharmacy machine said one thirty over eighty something, but I'd just speed-walked from the car, so I figured that one didn't count.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): This reading's the one we'll use. He'll be right in.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hey, sorry, this computer's crawling. What brings you in?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): The sneezing, mostly. Itchy eyes and a runny nose. It shows up every spring and I finally decided to deal with it instead of just buying tissues in bulk.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hold on, the screen blanked. Say that again?

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Sneezing, itchy eyes, runny nose, every spring. I've had it since I was nineteen and I'm thirty four now, so, uh, fifteen years of the same thing. This round started the first week of April.
[SEG0010] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The eyes have been bad for two months though. She's been rubbing them constantly, since March.

[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that March thing was a cold, I told you. The itchy eyes from the allergies started the first week of April, so three weeks, not two months. And I don't rub them constantly. Only after I've been outside when the pollen is high, because rubbing makes the itch worse.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, two months or three weeks? I was clicking the wrong tab.
[SEG0013] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I still think two months. She was at the sink rubbing her eyes in March.

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Different illness. Three weeks for this. I know because my birthday's the last week of March and I was fine at dinner, I even had the spicy pasta and my nose wasn't running that night.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay, I'll put it down as somewhere between three weeks and a couple of months. We won't fight it out today. What do you take for it?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Cetrizine, sorry, cetirizine, the generic, ten milligrams. I take it sometimes. Not every day. More like three or four days a week, when the sneezing fits are bad, and I skip it if we're just staying inside.
[SEG0017] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She takes it every morning. The bottle's on the counter every single day.

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The bottle lives on the counter because I'm lazy about putting it away. I am not taking it every day. Three or four days a week. It takes the edge off the sneezing. It does basically nothing for my eyes.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ten milligrams, three or four days a week. Say the name once more? I typed cetrizine.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Cetirizine. Ten milligrams. By mouth. Three or four days a week.

[SEG0021] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Her sister takes biotin, five thousand micrograms, for her hair. We asked if maybe you should try that. And I take metformin, five hundred milligrams twice a day, for my diabetes, but that's me, not her.

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I never took her biotin. And his metformin isn't mine. My sister's allergic to dust, dust mites, the whole indoor thing. Mine is outdoor, spring trees. Totally different pattern.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any wheezing? Any shortness of breath?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No wheeze at all. No shortness of breath. I can walk the dog around the block, I just sneeze the entire loop. Chest feels normal.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any reactions to medicines? Drug allergies?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never. I have taken a penicillin type, amoxicillin, for a sinus infection years ago, and I was completely fine. No rash, nothing. I can take pretty much everything.

[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me look. Password again, of course. Alright. Nasal mucosa is pale and boggy, clear drainage. Conjunctiva is injected, both eyes. Lungs are clear, I don't hear a wheeze.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): The dripping is worst in the morning, I can go through half a box of tissues before noon, and the air conditioning settles it if I stay in. Outside, especially by the oak tree on our corner, I get these sneezing fits, ten, sometimes twelve in a row. I actually counted.

[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. This sounds like seasonal allergic rhinitis, and allergic conjunctivitis with it. Working impression, not confirmed until we see the tests, but that's what I'm treating.

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I knew it was the spring thing. I just didn't know if you call it rhinitis or just allergies. I tell people allergies and they think I'm being dramatic, but the tissue budget is real, we buy the bulk box at Costco, which is a whole Saturday.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm changing the antihistamine. Stop the cetirizine today. Start fexofenadine, one hundred eighty milligrams, once a day, by mouth.

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Fexofenadine. Is that Allegra? My coworker says Allegra, or maybe she said something else, she gets sleepy and I don't want sleepy. Can you repeat the dose? I want it exact.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): One eighty milligrams once daily. Non-drowsy. And I'm adding olopatadine eye drops, one drop each eye, twice a day. Start both today.

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Olopatadine, one drop, both eyes, twice a day. Stop cetrizine, start the one eighty. If I mess up the drop and it runs down my cheek, do I do another one? I tried those drugstore redness drops once, the little white bottle, can't remember the name, they did nothing so I stopped.

[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): One drop is enough even if a little spills, don't double up. The nurse takes bloods Thursday morning, a specific IgE panel for trees, grass, and dust mite. No fasting, be here at eight, and you can take your medicines that morning, they won't affect this blood test.
[SEG0036] person_1 (NURSE): Thursday at 8, I'll draw it myself. No fasting, meds are fine.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): And I'll see you in two weeks to go over the results.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): If those are borderline we do skin testing. If the symptoms do not settle on the new meds, we might do a sinus CT. I'm not ordering either of those today.

[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Skin testing is the little scratches, right? My sister had that for her dust allergy and her arm blew up. I don't think I'm dust, I only fall apart April and May, sometimes into June if the pollen hangs on. I check the pollen app every morning with my coffee, which is probably too much coffee, but anyway.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): What was that last bit? I was in the scheduling screen.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing, the coffee. So the skin test only if the bloods are borderline, and the scan only if I don't settle. And the two week visit is definitely happening, not if.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. Two weeks is booked. Skin testing and the CT only if those conditions hit.
[SEG0043] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And she stops the cetirizine now, not after Thursday?
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stops today. Fexofenadine starts today, drops start today. Thursday is just the blood draw.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): What if the fexofenadine gives me a headache? I don't have a headache, I'm just, I read things and then I spiral. Sorry, I over-explain, my husband can vouch.
[SEG0046] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She does over-explain, yeah. I'm not dropping the two months thing, I know what I saw in March, but we can leave it. And I still think the cetirizine is daily.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): It was a cold, and the pill is not daily. Anyway. Thursday at eight, no fasting, I can take the new pill that morning. Then back in two weeks no matter what.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's the plan. If you get a rash or the eyes get dramatically worse, call us, but otherwise it's the two weeks.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Thursday at eight, then two weeks. Thanks. Sorry I talked your ear off.

spec.situation: Sneezing, itchy eyes and runny nose every spring; takes cetirizine 'sometimes'; sister is allergic to dust; no wheeze; doctor changes antihistamine and adds eye drops.

traps.happens: In the plan the doctor books some tests or visits for a definite time ('the nurse takes bloods Thursday morning', 'I'll see you in two weeks') and makes others conditional ('if those are borderline we do the third test', 'if it does not settle, a scan').
traps.label_rule: Booked or arranged = status planned. Only the hedged ones are conditional. Never mark a booked test conditional or 'if needed'. Instructions for the booked test (fasting, time, medicine timing) belong to that test's action, not a separate invented plan item.

traps.happens: The doctor asks about drug reactions. Variants (use ONE per encounter): (a) the patient says 'No, never, I have taken penicillin and everything' (no allergy); (b) the patient is unsure ('maybe the antibiotic or the painkiller, nobody told me which'); (c) a real allergy with the reaction described; (d) allergies are never asked.
traps.label_rule: (a) NO allergy entry: negative_findings 'Allergies' absent. (b) allergy with status uncertain, the substance as described, the reaction if said, plus an allergy_uncertain uncertainty. (c) allergy with the reaction. (d) nothing at all. NEVER list a medicine the patient has taken without a reaction as an allergy, and the plan must not prescribe a drug of a recorded allergy's family.

features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

omissions.text: Runny nose/sneezing symptoms are specifically triggered by outdoor spring tree pollen and the patient reports an outdoor pattern; by history she only 'falls apart' in April and May, sometimes into June if pollen persists, and is not bothered by indoor dust exposure. This contrasts with her sister's dust mite allergy.

The patient reported the seasonal problem has recurred every spring for 15 years since age 19; this duration/history is not reflected for the itchy eye symptom, which the patient specifically said began the first week of April this year (about 3 weeks), while the family member's '2 months' referred to a different March illness/cold.

Specific IgE panel timing/details were more specific than recorded: blood draw is Thursday at 8 AM, performed by the nurse, for trees, grass, and dust mite, with no fasting and medications allowed that morning because they will not affect this blood test.
